# The datasets {#sec-data}

Every dataset in this booklet is simulated by `scripts/make_data.R`, from seed
2025. Run `Rscript scripts/make_data.R` from the project root to regenerate all
of them; `data/PROVENANCE.txt` records when and with which R version.

Simulation is deliberate, for three reasons. The generating process is known, so
every diagnostic question has a checkable answer. No information governance
approval is needed, so the files can live in a public repository. And the
defects are the ones we chose, so they can be taught.

## `los_data.csv` — the training world

1000 admissions. Used in Exercises 1.2 and 1.3.

| Column | Meaning | Generating process |
|---|---|---|
| `Age` | years | Normal(60, 15), truncated below at 18, **not truncated above** |
| `Severity` | severity score, 1–10 | Normal(5.4, 2.07), clipped to [1, 10] |
| `LOS` | length of stay, days | $-8.5 + 0.94\,\text{Age} + 3.37\,\text{Severity} + \varepsilon$, $\varepsilon \sim N(0, 4.3)$ |

: {tbl-colwidths="[14,30,56]"}

**Known defects, retained on purpose.**

- The maximum age is just over 109, and 26 patients are aged 90 or more. Nothing
  truncates the upper tail, exactly as in extracts
  where a default or mistyped date of birth survives into the warehouse.
- Typical LOS is about 66 days, which is wrong for acute medicine by an order of
  magnitude.
- `LOS` is symmetric. Real length of stay is strongly right-skewed. This is the
  single most recognisable difference between this file and a real one.
- Severity piles up at exactly 1 and 10 because the draw is clipped, not
  bounded: 2.0% of rows sit at 1 and 1.6% at 10.

Both of the first two are the subject of Exercise 1.2, Task 1.

These parameters match the `los_data.csv` distributed in earlier years of the
module, so answers stated as ranges are unaffected by which copy a student has.

## `extract_A.csv`, `extract_B.csv`, `extract_C.csv` — the later extracts

400 admissions each. Used in Exercise 1.3. Students are told only that they are
monthly extracts taken after the model went live, and must diagnose what
changed. The mechanisms are in `scripts/make_data.R` and in the instructor
chapter.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Publishing note
`scripts/make_data.R` contains the answer to Exercise 1.3. If you publish the
student site from the same repository, either exclude `scripts/` from the
published output or accept that a determined student can read the key. Nothing
else in the booklet gives it away.
:::

## `los_data_skewed.csv` — the realistic variant

1000 admissions, same predictors, but LOS is drawn from a Gamma distribution
with a multiplicative mean, $\mathbb{E}[\text{LOS}] = \exp(0.15 + 0.012\,\text{Age} + 0.17\,\text{Severity})$,
shape 2. Median around four days, with a long right tail. Not used on Day 1;
it exists for the sessions on metrics and on generalised linear models, where
the difference between a symmetric and a skewed outcome changes the answer.

## `birthweight.csv` — the transfer task

600 pregnancies. `bpd` (biparietal diameter, mm) and `ad` (abdominal diameter,
mm) predict `bw` (birth weight, g) through
$-1700 + 30\,\text{bpd} + 25\,\text{ad} + \varepsilon$, $\varepsilon \sim N(0, 250)$.
Units and magnitudes are plausible; the numbers are invented. Used in Exercise
1.2 Task 4 so that students rerun the pipeline on columns whose names bear no
resemblance to the ones they just used.

## Using real data instead

Any of these can be swapped for a real dataset, and the booklet's structure
survives it, but two things change and should be said out loud when you do it.
The known answer disappears, so the self-checks that compare against a key
(`check_shift_answers()`) no longer apply; and the defects become the ones the
extract happens to have rather than the ones the exercise needs. Teaching
diagnosis first on data with a known answer, then on real data, is the order
that works.
